Chemistry, Physics and Physical Science
PX 2000 - Physics 1, Algebra-based
Credits: 3
This is the first course in the non-calculus-based physics sequence, which presents an overview of the fundamental
concepts and quantitative methods of physics. This course provides a foundational understanding of classical Newton
mechanics, which describes the motion of objects and the forces that cause them to move. Topics include linear and
rotational motion, forces and Newton’s laws, gravitation, kinetic and potential energy, and momentum.
Prerequisites
MA 2090
or equivalent, completed with grade of “C” or better
When Offered:
Every semester
Note:
Previously named “CP 2220 Structure of Physics I”
PX 2001 - Physics 1, Algebra Based Lab
Credits: 1
This laboratory course provides students with hands-on experiences to complement the theoretical concepts introduced
in the corresponding lecture course, PX 2000. Through a series of experiments and simulations emphasizing
experimental techniques, data analysis, and error estimation, students will explore fundamental principles of
Newtonian mechanics, including motion, forces, energy, and momentum.

PX 2700 - Wave Motion: Light and Sound
Credits: 4
An introductory course on the science of waves in light and sound and their applications to modern forms of technology
that directly impact our lives, such as wireless communication, image recognition, and remote sensory data collection.
Students learn the basic concepts through activities with microcomputer-based laboratory (mbl) technology, designed to
explore applications with inquiry-based tasks using sensors and mobile devices to collect and analyze data.
Prerequisites
MA 1020
PX 2900 - Astronomy
Credits: 3
Explore the wonders of the universe in this introductory survey of astronomy. From the night sky to the origin of the
universe, this course features evidence-based reasoning, critical thinking, and use of theoretical models and
observations. Topics include apparent sky motions, telescopes, planets, structure and evolution of the solar system, stars,
black holes, galaxies, and cosmology.
Prerequisites
MA 1020
PX 2901 - Astronomy Laboratory
Credits: 1
This introduction to observational astronomy is the lab associated to PX 2900
. This course addresses the basic techniques of unaided astronomical observing as well as observation with a telescope.

PX 3900 - Experimental Physics and Electronics Lab
Credits: 3
This course provides a hands-on introduction to the electronics and instrumentation used in experimental physics.
Topics include DC and AC circuits, filters, power supplies, transistors, diodes, operational amplifiers, and analog to
digital converters and logic. This is primarily a laboratory class, but time will also be spent in and out of the class on the
mathematical description of the circuits and instruments, as well as discussions of the theory underlying modern
components, such as the diode and transistor.
Prerequisites

Credits: 3

heat, thermal equilibrium, reversible and irreversible processes, entropy, and free energy. Applications such as ideal
gases, heat engines, refrigerators, and phase transitions will be covered.

PX 4200 - Quantum Mechanics
Credits: 3
This course is an introduction to the concepts and methods of quantum mechanics. Topics will include the postulates of
quantum mechanics, Schrödinger’s equation, Dirac notation, measurements, operators and observables, angular
momentum and spin, and the exclusion principle. Applications will include harmonic oscillator, the hydrogen atom,
and scattering.
Prerequisites
PX 3000
with grade of “C” or better, MA 2320
When Offered:
Spring of even-numbered years
PX 4300 - Applied Quantum Mechanics
Credits: 3
This course is a survey of the basic principles of quantum mechanics with a focus on applications in modern, nuclear,
and molecular physics. Topics include an overview of quantum mechanics, the hydrogen atom, electronic structure, and
the quantum theory of atoms and molecules. Emphasis is placed on electronic structure, spectroscopy, and
computational methods. Theoretical concepts are applied to real-world problems in physics, chemistry, and materials
science throughout the semester.
Prerequisites
CP 2130
completed with a grade of “C” or better; MA 2320
completed with a grade of “C” or better, PX 2300
or PX 2100
completed with a grade of “C” or better.

PX 4600 - Applied Mechanics
Credits: 3
This course explores statics and dynamics of rigid bodies and of stress and strain applied to “real” materials with
elasticity and finite strength. Topics include simple equilibrium, structural analysis, inertia tensors, centroids, energy
and momentum, and strength of materials, as well as, concepts of stress and strain in structural members experiencing
tension, compression, shear, bending, and twisting.
Prerequisites

with grade of “C” or better, MA 2320

condensed matter, biophysics, astrophysics, cosmology, or string theory.

11/7/26, 2:14 PM Course Descriptions - SUNY Old Westbury
Credits: 3
Econophysics is the application of ideas from statistical physics to the financial markets. In this course, the dynamics of
markets are analyzed from a physics perspective. The statistical methods needed to model financial markets are
introduced: classes of Brownian motion, probability distributions and limit theorems. Comparison with other physical
systems are used to develop intuitions for these methods. Stochastic models for price dynamics and time-dependent
models for equity valuations, such as the Black-Scholes equation, used in options pricing, are developed. Real world
markets, such as equity stock markets, fixed income markets, and commodities markets, are considered.
Prerequisites
PX 4100
, BU 4762
, CS 2510
When Offered:
As needed
PX 5500 - Senior Seminar 1
Credits: 1
The first semester of a year-long capstone course for physics majors. Students engage in independent research projects
under the guidence of faculty mentors, culminating in a written article, a poster presented at Research Day, and an oral
presentation to faculty and peers. The course covers literature reviews, scientific writing, and effective presentation
skills.
Prerequisites
Senior standing or permission of the instructor
When Offered:
Fall Only

records.title: Applied Quantum Mechanics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 3
This course is a survey of the basic principles of quantum mechanics with a focus on applications in modern, nuclear,
and molecular physics. Topics include an overview of quantum mechanics, the hydrogen atom, electronic structure, and
the quantum theory of atoms and molecules. Emphasis is placed on electronic structure, spectroscopy, and
computational methods. Theoretical concepts are applied to real-world problems in physics, chemistry, and materials
science throughout the semester.
Prerequisites
CP 2130
completed with a grade of “C” or better; MA 2320
completed with a grade of “C” or better, PX 2300
or PX 2100
completed with a grade of “C” or better.

When Offered:
Spring of even-numbered years
Note:
This course is cross-listed with CP 4710 Physical Chemistry II.

records.title: Applied Mechanics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 3
This course explores statics and dynamics of rigid bodies and of stress and strain applied to “real” materials with
elasticity and finite strength. Topics include simple equilibrium, structural analysis, inertia tensors, centroids, energy
and momentum, and strength of materials, as well as, concepts of stress and strain in structural members experiencing
tension, compression, shear, bending, and twisting.
Prerequisites
PX 3000
with grade of “C” or better, MA 2320

records.title: Econophysics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 3
Econophysics is the application of ideas from statistical physics to the financial markets. In this course, the dynamics of
markets are analyzed from a physics perspective. The statistical methods needed to model financial markets are
introduced: classes of Brownian motion, probability distributions and limit theorems. Comparison with other physical
systems are used to develop intuitions for these methods. Stochastic models for price dynamics and time-dependent
models for equity valuations, such as the Black-Scholes equation, used in options pricing, are developed. Real world
markets, such as equity stock markets, fixed income markets, and commodities markets, are considered.
Prerequisites
PX 4100
, BU 4762
, CS 2510
When Offered:
As needed
